blocks.text: Text columns are the messiest data type of all, since there is no schema enforcing what a human, or another system, typed into a free text field. A numeric column can only really be off by wrong values, but a string column can be off in a dozen small, silent ways at once.

items: Extra internal whitespace: "New York" with several spaces where there should be one.
Mixed casing: "john SMITH" instead of a consistent style.
Special characters and punctuation noise: stray quotes, ampersands, or HTML entities scraped from the web.
Embedded control characters: a newline or tab character hidden inside a single field.

blocks.text: Every pandas string operation goes through the .str accessor, which applies a vectorized version of a normal Python string method to every row in a column at once.

code.content:
df['name'] = df['name'].str.strip()          # remove leading/trailing whitespace
df['name'] = df['name'].str.lower()           # normalize case
df['name'] = df['name'].str.replace(',', '')  # remove a specific character
mask = df['email'].str.contains('@')          # find rows matching a pattern
domain = df['email'].str.extract(r'@(.+)$')   # pull out a substring

blocks.text: A "name" column has extra whitespace, inconsistent casing, and one row with an embedded newline character. Cleaning it end to end with a single chained expression handles all three at once.
Regular expressions are the general purpose tool once simple string methods are not enough. Two patterns come up constantly in cleaning work.

items: \s+ matches one or more whitespace characters in a row, useful for collapsing multiple spaces into a single space.
[^a-zA-Z0-9\s] matches anything that is not a letter, digit, or whitespace, useful for stripping punctuation.

code.content:
import re
text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text)                    # collapse whitespace
text = re.sub(r'[^a-zA-Z0-9\s]', '', text)           # strip punctuation

# the pandas equivalent, applied to a whole column at once
df['col'] = df['col'].str.replace(r'\s+', ' ', regex=True)

blocks.text: Data scraped from the web frequently carries leftover HTML markup or entities like & that should have been plain text. A simple regex strips most of this in one pass.

code.content:
df['col'] = df['col'].str.replace(r'<[^>]+>', '', regex=True)  # strip HTML tags
df['col'] = df['col'].str.replace('&', '&', regex=False)     # decode a common entity

blocks.text: A subtler issue: the same visible character, like an accented e, can be represented by different underlying byte sequences in Unicode. Two strings that look completely identical to a human can compare as not equal in code because of this.

code.content:
import unicodedata
clean = unicodedata.normalize('NFC', text)  # collapse to a single canonical representation

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: A name typed with a pre composed accented character and the same name typed with a base letter plus a separate accent mark look identical on screen but are different strings until normalized.

items: Forgetting regex=True: str.replace() treats its pattern as a literal string by default, a pattern like \s+ does nothing unless regex=True is passed explicitly.
Lowercasing without stripping: applying str.lower() but forgetting str.strip() leaves lingering whitespace differences that still cause values which look identical to be treated as distinct.
Strip leading and trailing whitespace on every text column.
Collapse internal multiple spaces to one.
Strip or decode HTML markup if the data came from the web.
Normalize Unicode if names or text involve accented characters.
